definition: Total (whole-body) percentage body fat measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (Hologic QDR 4500A) in examined NHANES participants. Values are survey-weighted and use multiple imputation for missing or invalid DXA scans. Row used: males, all races and ethnicities, age 20 years and older, crude.
caveat: The question asks for the top 1% leanest men, which is p1 on a lower-is-better scale. No credible population source publishes p1 for adult male body fat. The best national source, the NHANES 1999-2004 DXA tables, stops at p5 (17.4% for US men 20+; 15.5% for men 20-39), so the site will have to extrapolate below p5. I found only one source on this exact definition (Hologic DXA, US men 20+, population-weighted). Kelly, Wilson & Heymsfield 2009 (PLoS ONE, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0007038) publishes DXA %fat reference percentiles from the same NHANES 1999-2004 scans, broken out by ethnicity only. It is not independent of the CDC report, so it is left out of sources. Comparison, not for averaging: Imboden et al. 2017 (PLoS ONE, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0175110) measured Caucasian adults on GE Lunar Prodigy or iDXA scanners at two US university labs. This is a convenience sample, not population-weighted, and GE and Hologic scanners give systematically different %fat readings. Its table labels the leanest value as the '90th' percentile (fitness-ranking convention). Rewritten in conventional low-is-lean terms, its men's p10 is 11.0% at 20-29 (n=384, mean 21.1 ± SD 8.3, median 20.2), 11.2% at 30-39, 15.8% at 40-49, 20.0% at 50-59, 21.0% at 60-69 and 23.0% at 70-79. Other methods (BIA, skinfolds, smart scales, calipers) are not comparable to DXA and were not used. The NHANES data are 20 years old, and US adiposity has risen since, so current percentiles are probably somewhat higher. Body fat rises with age, so an age-specific band (20-39) gives a leaner threshold than the all-adult row.

sources.measures: Mean silent reading rate of healthy adult native speakers aged 17-60 reading normal text for comprehension, pooled across 190 published studies (1901-2019, mostly English, predominantly university students). sources.notes: 238 wpm is the unweighted mean across studies (95% CI 230-246); 235 is the MEDIAN OF STUDY MEANS, not a person-level median. SD 51.2 is the between-study SD of study means, not the between-person SD. Weighted subset (87 studies, 10,201 participants, with reported SDs): mean 247.5 wpm, SD 47.4. Mean for fiction 260 wpm, non-fiction 238 wpm. Paper states 'most adults fall in the range of 175-300 wpm' for non-fiction and '200-320 wpm' for fiction; this is a descriptive range, not a stated percentile. definition: Mean silent reading rate of healthy adult native speakers aged 17-60 reading normal text for comprehension, pooled across 190 published studies (1901-2019, mostly English, predominantly university students). Unweighted random-effects mean of study-level means. Words counted as published by each study (no character normalisation).
caveat: No credible source publishes a 99th percentile (or any percentile) of adult silent reading speed; the best sources give only means, between-study SDs, and descriptive ranges, so a top-1% value cannot be reported without deriving it. The SCF measures it per family among families that hold education loans, not per individual borrower, and a family can contain more than one borrower. Among all families the median is $0, because only about 22% hold student debt. One comparison is the Federal Reserve SHED (Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2024, May 2025, https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2025-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2024-higher-education-and-student-loans.htm). It is individual-level and self-reported, counts debt for the respondent's own education only, and publishes the median only as a bracket: 'between $20,000 and $24,999'. It also reports that 28% of borrowers owed under $10,000 and most owed under $25,000. That puts it in line with the SCF, but it is a different unit of observation and is left out of sources. The Cleveland Fed Economic Commentary 2024-10 restates the SCF figures (about $25,000 median, $47,000 mean) and is not independent. The SCF is known to understate aggregate student debt relative to Fed G.19 and NY Fed credit-bureau totals, by roughly 25% in one secondary estimate. Neither official source publishes p90 or p99 values. The research step returned the values in thousands and averaged the 2019 and 2022 waves; the grid was corrected to the 2022 median in dollars at build review.

definition: VO2max measured directly by cardiopulmonary exercise testing (gas exchange) on a maximal treadmill test. Sample is US adults aged 20-79 without cardiovascular disease, from 8 US laboratories. Percentiles are given by sex and decade of age.
caveat: Neither source publishes a 99th percentile. FRIEND 2015 stops at p95 (59.8 mL/kg/min for US men 30-39), and HUNT 3 gives only mean 49.1 and SD 7.5 for Norwegian men 30-39. Any p99 figure would be an extrapolation the site has to make. The two samples also differ: the HUNT 3 mean (49.1) sits well above the FRIEND median (42.4), so the cohorts are not interchangeable and a plain average will blur that difference. Neither is a random national sample. FRIEND is US lab-tested adults without cardiovascular disease, and HUNT 3 is healthy Norwegian volunteers, so treating them as 'world' is a stretch. The 2022 FRIEND update (Kaminsky et al., Mayo Clin Proc 97(2):285-293, n=16,278 treadmill tests from 34 US labs) reports treadmill standards 1.5-4.6 mL/kg/min lower than the 2015 values. Its men 30-39 table could not be retrieved, and secondary blogs quoting it disagree (medians of 38.6 and 39.7 both appear), so it is left out of sources. Excluded on definition: (1) Cooper Institute/Cooper Clinic tables (reprinted by Garmin, p95 'Superior' = 54.0 for men 30-39) use VO2max predicted from treadmill time, not measured gas exchange. (2) Peterman et al. 2021 JAHA FRIEND tables cover patients with cardiovascular disease (men 30-39 treadmill p90 = 40.3), not the general population. (3) Smartwatch VO2 max estimates (Garmin, Apple) are algorithmic estimates on a different basis. Elite endurance athletes routinely exceed 70-80 mL/kg/min, so the true population p99 is probably above the FRIEND p95, but no credible source states it.

sources.measures: Estimated number of English lemmas known by American native English speakers aged 20. Lemmas are uninflected words with proper nouns excluded, taken from a list of 61,800 entries. Knowledge was measured by yes/no word recognition with pseudoword correction in an online crowdsourced test.
sources.notes: n = 221,268 is the total number of individuals tested (265,346 sessions), not the age-20 American subsample, which the paper does not state in the parts read. The abstract gives the range as 27,000 lemmas (lowest 5%) to 52,000 (highest 5%). Table 4 gives the 20-year-old upper value as 51,700, and that value is used here. For 60-year-olds the paper gives a median of 48,200 lemmas and a 5th to 95th range of 35,100 to 56,400. definition: Estimated number of English lemmas known by American native English speakers aged 20. Lemmas are uninflected words with proper nouns excluded, taken from a list of 61,800 entries. Knowledge was measured by yes/no word recognition with pseudoword correction in an online crowdsourced test.
caveat: The question asks for the top 1% of adults, but the only source on this definition publishes no value above the 95th percentile. Its p95 for 20-year-olds is about 52,000 lemmas and for 60-year-olds 56,400 lemmas, so the true p99 lies above those figures, capped by the 61,800-lemma test list. The sample is self-selected online test takers, restricted to American native speakers and split by age. It is not a representative sample of all adults, and non-native speakers are excluded. Comparison on a different scale, not averaged: myvocab.info (BRAVE project) counts word families with an adaptive IRT test on about 29,000 self-selected native speakers. It reports p25 14,400, p50 17,100, p75 19,900 and p90 22,700 word families, with no p95 or p99. Its word-family definition differs from Brysbaert's base words, and Brysbaert's word-family median is 11,100. Older rule-of-thumb estimates (Nation; Goulden, Nation & Read 1990) put educated native speakers near 20,000 word families. Those figures are also word families and are not comparable with lemmas.
